Treatment converts better than control across all visitors and within every department.
Overall, control averages 0.60 conversion and treatment averages 0.40 — suggesting control wins at the aggregate level.

The reversal between the overall and department-level results is a known statistical paradox: the department mix likely differs between treatment and control, making the aggregate comparison misleading.

Overall, the treatment group converts at a lower rate than control, but within each department the treatment consistently outperforms control — a classic Simpson's Paradox that argues against a blanket rollout without further investigation.
The overall numbers favour control, yet every individual department tells the opposite story, meaning the aggregate result is misleading and the rollout decision cannot safely rest on it.
Taken as a whole, the treatment group converts at 0.6 and the control group at 0.4, so treatment is better overall.
This reversal between the overall and per-department results is a sign that department composition is unevenly distributed across the two groups, making the aggregate comparison unreliable.
Unbalanced assignment is the most likely cause of the conflicting signals and must be ruled out first.
Per-department results consistently favour treatment and are the more reliable basis for a rollout decision.
Net revenue retention has declined significantly over the past year, driven entirely by expansion slowing and contraction rising, with no logo churn or new customer additions to offset it.

Net revenue retention fell to 106.5% for the 12 months to 31 Oct 2026, down from 122.7% a year earlier — a drop of 16.2 points — signalling that existing customers are expanding much less than before.
Contraction is the primary drag on net revenue retention and the main risk to sustaining year-over-year growth.
With no new logos, any future contraction or churn has no new revenue to offset it.
